content.title: About
content.content: Flourless chocolate cake is a dense, moist dessert made without wheat flour. Instead, almond or other nut flours, cocoa powder, and egg whites are used, giving the cake a rich chocolate flavor and a tender crumb. It is a popular choice for those avoiding gluten.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Flourless cakes first appeared in the early 20th century as a gluten‑free alternative.
Almond or hazelnut flour adds a subtle nutty aroma to the cake.
The cake is often topped with dark chocolate ganache, fresh berries, or toasted nuts for contrast.
Without flour, the cake has a lower glycemic index than traditional cakes.
Some vegan versions replace eggs with aquafaba, the liquid from canned chickpeas.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Dark chocolate provides flavonoids that help combat oxidative stress.

items.title: Low in gluten
items.content: The absence of wheat flour makes the cake safe for people with gluten intolerance.

items.title: Source of healthy fats
items.content: Nut flours contribute monounsaturated fats beneficial for heart health.

items.title: Contains protein
items.content: Eggs and nut flours add a notable amount of animal and plant protein.

items.title: Mood‑boosting
items.content: Chocolate stimulates serotonin production, which can improve mood.

items.title: Nut allergy
items.content: Almond or other nut flours may trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: Chocolate and nuts make the cake calorie‑rich, so portion control is advised.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Many recipes contain added sugar, which may be a concern for diabetics.

items.title: Caffeine content
items.content: Dark chocolate contains caffeine, which can affect sleep if consumed in large amounts.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the cake in slices, often accompanied by berry coulis, whipped cream, or a scoop of ice cream. It can be enjoyed chilled or gently warmed in the microwave.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the cake in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days. For longer storage, freeze it in a sealed bag for up to 2 months. Allow it to thaw at room temperature for about 30 minutes before serving.

chicken-or-turkey-with-cheese-sauce.title: Chicken or turkey with cheese sauce

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken and turkey are lean sources of protein that are often served with a rich cheese sauce. The dish combines juicy poultry meat with a creamy sauce made from cheese, milk, and spices, making it a favorite in both home cooking and restaurant menus.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The cheese sauce can be made from various cheeses: cheddar, mozzarella, parmesan, or processed cheese.
In the United States the dish is often baked, while in Europe it is commonly served as a piece of meat topped with sauce.
Turkey contains slightly less fat than chicken, but both birds are rich in B‑vitamins.
Cheese sauces are frequently enhanced with mustard or paprika for extra flavor.
The dish cooks quickly: the meat is sautéed and the sauce is simmered for a few minutes.

items.title: High-quality protein
items.content: Chicken and turkey provide complete protein needed for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Poultry is a good source of niacin (B3) and vitamin B6, which support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: The cheese sauce adds calcium, important for bone and dental health.

items.title: Low saturated fat (when using low‑fat cheese)
items.content: Choosing reduced‑fat cheese varieties can keep saturated fat levels modest.

items.title: Essential minerals
items.content: The sauce often contributes phosphorus and zinc, which aid immunity and energy metabolism.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Cheese sauce may trigger reactions in people with lactose intolerance or dairy allergies.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Cheeses can be high in salt; monitor added salt during preparation.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The creamy sauce increases the dish’s calories, so serve in moderate portions.

items.title: Thorough cooking required
items.content: Poultry must be fully cooked to eliminate the risk of salmonella.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot, typically with a side of potatoes, rice, or vegetables. Slice the meat, coat it with cheese sauce, and optionally bake until golden. Garnish with fresh herbs or spices for added aroma.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Reheat thoroughly until bubbling. The dish can be frozen for up to 2 months if portioned beforehand.

content.title: About
content.content: Cough drops are small pastille tablets that contain soothing and expectorant ingredients such as menthol, eucalyptus, honey, thyme extract, or other plant extracts. They are intended to relieve dry or irritated cough, soften the throat lining, and reduce discomfort.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cough drops are popular for travel because they are portable and do not require water.
Some recipes include natural honey, which has antibacterial properties.
Menthol, a common ingredient, creates a cooling sensation and eases breathing.
In Soviet pharmacy practice, cough drops were often combined with herbal decoctions like sage.
Modern sugar‑free versions use sweeteners such as stevia to lower calorie content.

items.title: Soothes irritated throat
items.content: Components like honey and plant extracts form a protective layer that reduces irritation.

items.title: Expectorant effect
items.content: Eucalyptus and menthol help thin mucus, making it easier to clear.

items.title: Relieves dry cough
items.content: Mild sweeteners and aromatic agents lower the reflex cough response.

items.title: Calming effect
items.content: The scent of menthol and eucalyptus provides a mild soothing sensation for the airways.

items.title: Convenient use
items.content: Drops can be taken anytime without the need for water.

items.title: Allergy to ingredients
items.content: Honey, plant extracts, or flavorings may trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Traditional drops contain sugar, which may be unsuitable for people with diabetes.

items.title: Menthol overuse
items.content: High amounts of menthol can cause mucosal irritation or dizziness.

items.title: Not for children under 3
items.content: Drops pose a choking hazard for young children.

items.title: Interaction with medications
items.content: Some herbal components may affect the action of certain drugs, for example by altering mucus consistency.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Allow the cough drop to dissolve slowly in the mouth, letting it fully melt. Do not swallow whole. Typical dosage is 1‑2 drops every 2‑3 hours, not exceeding 6‑8 per day. Consult a healthcare professional if you have a chronic cough or underlying conditions.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store drops in a cool, dry place in a tightly sealed container to prevent moisture absorption. At temperatures above 25 °C they may soften and lose shape. Observe the expiration date on the package and discard after it passes.

green-beans-frozen-cooked-fat-added-ns-a.title: Green beans, frozen, cooked, fat added, NS

content.title: About
content.content: Green beans (Phaseolus vulgaris) are young pods harvested before the seeds fully mature. This product is blanched, frozen, and has a plant-based fat added, with the fat type listed as NS (not specified). It offers a quick‑cook convenience while retaining most of the vegetable’s nutrients.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Green beans are a good source of B‑vitamins, vitamin C, and potassium.
Freezing immediately after cooking preserves their bright color and crisp texture.
Added fat enhances absorption of fat‑soluble nutrients such as vitamin K.
Green beans are common in Asian and Mediterranean cuisines as side dishes and salads.
Several cultivars exist, differing in pod size and shape.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports healthy digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Contains vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C acts as an antioxidant that helps protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: Potassium and magnesium help maintain normal blood pressure, and the added plant fat may provide beneficial monounsaturated fats.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: When consumed in moderation, it fits well into calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Source of plant protein
items.content: Protein contributes to muscle maintenance, especially when combined with other protein sources.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to beans.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Prepared versions may contain added salt; people monitoring sodium should check the label.

items.title: Unspecified fat type
items.content: Since the fat type is listed as NS, those with sensitivities should verify the ingredient list.

items.title: Food safety after thawing
items.content: If thawed and left at room temperature too long, bacterial growth can occur.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Thaw the beans in the microwave or gently on the stovetop, then heat until hot. They can be added to soups, stews, salads, pasta dishes, or served as a side seasoned with herbs, soy sauce, or lemon juice.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the frozen product at –18 °C (0 °F) or lower. Once thawed, use within 1–2 days and store in the refrigerator at 0–4 °C. Do not refreeze.

content.title: About
content.content: Dried papaya consists of thin slices of ripe papaya (Carica papaya) that have been dehydrated. The process retains most of the fruit’s vitamins, minerals, and its characteristic sweet‑tart flavor. It is lightweight, shelf‑stable, and makes a convenient healthy snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Papaya originates from tropical Central and South America but is now cultivated in Asia, Africa, and the Caribbean.
Dried pieces are commonly used in muesli, granola, and energy bars.
Papaya contains the enzyme papain, which helps break down proteins.
Traditional medicine uses papaya to aid digestion and reduce inflammation.
When stored properly, dried papaya can last up to 12 months.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Dried papaya retains a high level of vitamin C, supporting the immune system and acting as an antioxidant.

items.title: Source of beta‑carotene
items.content: Beta‑carotene converts to vitamin A in the body, essential for vision and skin health.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: The papain enzyme aids protein digestion, making it easier on the stomach.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes regular bowel movements and helps you feel fuller longer.

items.title: Mineral content
items.content: Papaya provides potassium, magnesium, and iron, which are important for overall bodily functions.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to papaya.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Dried fruit concentrates natural sugars, so it should be consumed in moderation, especially by people with diabetes.

items.title: Possible additives
items.content: Some brands add preservatives; always check the ingredient list.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Dried papaya can be eaten straight from the pack, added to oatmeal, yogurt, baked goods, smoothies, or tossed into salads. For a softer texture, briefly soak in warm water before use.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For extended storage, refrigerate. Discard if it becomes sticky, develops an off‑odor, or shows mold.

content.title: About
content.content: Parsley (Petroselinum crispum) is an annual herb widely used as a culinary garnish. Fresh parsley has bright green leaves, a fragrant, slightly bitter taste and a crisp texture. It is eaten raw, added to salads, soups, sauces and as a garnish for many dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Parsley belongs to the Apiaceae family and is closely related to celery and dill.
There are two main varieties: curly leaf and flat‑leaf (Italian), the latter being more flavorful.
In ancient Roman medicine parsley was used as a breath freshener.
Its high chlorophyll content makes it a popular addition to detox smoothies.
Parsley is sometimes credited with mild diuretic properties.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Fresh parsley provides over 100 % of the daily value of vitamin C per 100 g, supporting immune function and antioxidant defense.

items.title: High in vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting and bone health; parsley supplies more than 600 % of the DV per 100 g.

items.title: Folate source
items.content: Folate is needed for DNA synthesis and is especially important during pregnancy.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Parsley contains flavonoids such as quercetin and kaempferol, as well as carotenoids, which help combat oxidative stress.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: It provides potassium, iron and magnesium, supporting heart and muscle function.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to parsley, ranging from skin itching to swelling.

items.title: High vitamin K intake
items.content: Because of its vitamin K content, excessive consumption may interfere with anticoagulant medication.

items.title: Oxalates
items.content: Parsley contains oxalates, which in large amounts can contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible people.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Use fresh parsley by chopping it into salads, sauces (pesto, gremolata), soups, omelets and smoothies. It can be sprinkled over finished dishes for color and flavor. For a milder taste, briefly blanch the leaves.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh parsley in the refrigerator in a damp paper towel or in a glass of water covered with plastic wrap. It stays fresh for 5‑7 days. For longer storage, chop and freeze the leaves in airtight bags.

content.title: About
content.content: Pierogi are a traditional Slavic dish consisting of boiled or fried dough parcels filled with a wide variety of fillings. The dough is usually made from wheat flour, water, eggs, and salt. Fillings can be sweet (cottage cheese, berries, apples) or savory (meat, potatoes, cabbage, mushrooms). Pierogi are commonly served hot with sour cream or butter.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The word “pierogi” comes from the Old Slavic root meaning “feast” or “celebration”.
Hundreds of regional variations exist across Russia, Ukraine, and Poland, each with its own typical fillings and shapes.
Ukrainian “varenyky” are considered a type of pierogi but are made without yeast dough.
In Poland, pierogi are a national staple and are often served with fried onions and sour cream.
During the Soviet era, pierogi were a common, inexpensive school cafeteria meal.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Whole‑grain dough provides slow‑release energy, helping to maintain satiety.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Meat, cottage cheese, or legume fillings add substantial animal and plant protein.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Both the dough and many fillings contain B1, B2, and B6 vitamins that support metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Pierogi can supply iron, zinc, and magnesium, especially when meat or leafy‑green fillings are used.

items.title: Probiotic potential
items.content: When made with a sourdough starter, the dough may contribute beneficial gut bacteria.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: The dough and rich fillings make pierogi calorie‑dense, so they should be eaten in moderation.

items.title: Salt and fat
items.content: Savory fillings often contain a lot of salt and saturated fat, which may be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: The dough contains gluten, and fillings may include dairy, nuts, or seafood, which can trigger allergies.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: If left at room temperature too long, especially meat‑filled pierogi, they can become a breeding ground for bacteria.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pierogi are served hot, typically with sour cream, melted butter, or a drizzle of vinegar. They can be enjoyed as a main dish or paired with a salad. Sweet versions are often dusted with powdered sugar or topped with fruit sauces.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked pierogi in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze them in freezer‑safe bags; reheat in the oven or microwave before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Soup, Hot and Sour (1909) is a classic Asian broth known for its bright tangy‑spicy flavor. Made from chicken or vegetable stock, it is seasoned with soy sauce, vinegar, ginger, garlic, chili peppers and often includes tofu, mushrooms, seaweed and scallions.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish earned its name in the early 20th century when Beijing restaurants began experimenting with the balance of sour and hot.
It is traditionally served with rice noodles or plain rice, and sometimes topped with a poached egg.
Original recipes use rice vinegar, but many regions substitute lemon or lime juice.
Spiciness is adjusted with the amount of chili paste (e.g., Sichuan sauce) or fresh chilies.
The soup is considered a “warming” dish, often served in cold weather to boost body heat.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Ingredients such as tofu and mushrooms provide B1, B2 and B6, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Garlic and ginger have antioxidant and anti‑inflammatory properties.

items.title: May lower cholesterol
items.content: Moderate amounts of soy sauce can help reduce LDL cholesterol levels.

items.title: Aids digestion
items.content: Vinegar stimulates gastric juice production, while spices accelerate digestive processes.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: The broth supplies fluids and electrolytes, especially beneficial in chilly climates.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Soy sauce adds significant salt; low‑sodium versions are recommended for people with hypertension.

items.title: Spicy food sensitivity
items.content: Large amounts of chili can irritate the stomach in individuals with sensitive digestion.

items.title: Soy allergy
items.content: Tofu and soy sauce may trigger allergic reactions in susceptible individuals.

items.title: Acid reflux
items.content: Vinegar and hot spices can exacerbate heartburn symptoms.

content.title: How to Serve
content.content: Serve the hot soup in a deep bowl, garnish with fresh scallions, cilantro and lime wedges. Optional toppings include a boiled egg, fried tofu cubes, or seaweed for added texture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Reheat gently, adding a splash of water or broth to restore the desired consistency.

content.title: About
content.content: Whole grain fruit waffles are a ready‑to‑eat frozen product made from whole‑grain flour, berries or fruit pieces, and a modest amount of sugar. They feature a crisp golden exterior and a soft, aromatic interior, retaining much of the fiber and vitamins thanks to the whole grain and fruit components.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Whole‑grain waffles contain more dietary fiber than traditional white‑flour waffles.
Fruits such as blueberry, strawberry or apple retain a portion of their antioxidants even after freezing.
The waffles can be stored in the freezer and cooked quickly in a toaster or microwave.
In several countries they are marketed as a "grab‑and‑go" breakfast and are popular among athletes.
Flash‑freezing technology preserves texture and flavor without the need for added preservatives.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain flour provides dietary fiber that supports healthy digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Whole grains contain thiamine, niacin and folate, essential for energy metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidants from fruit
items.content: Berries and fruit add vitamin C and polyphenols that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Lower glycemic impact
items.content: The combination of whole grain and fruit leads to a slower rise in blood sugar compared with regular waffles.

items.title: Quick energy source
items.content: Carbohydrates from the grain and fruit are readily available, making the waffles convenient before workouts or as a snack.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The product contains wheat, so individuals with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity should choose a gluten‑free alternative.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: While moderate, the sugar should be accounted for by those monitoring blood glucose levels.

items.title: Risk of under‑heating
items.content: If not heated properly, the waffles may remain cold inside, increasing the risk of food‑borne illness.

items.title: Preservatives in long‑term storage
items.content: Some brands add small amounts of preservatives to extend shelf life; check the label if you are sensitive.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Toast the frozen waffles for 2–3 minutes until golden and crisp. Serve with yogurt, honey, nut butter, or fresh berries to enhance flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the waffles in a sealed bag in the freezer at –18 °C. After thawing, consume within 24 hours and do not leave at room temperature for more than 2 hours.
